title: AlphaZero against Stockfish, 2017: space and patience
outcomes: Counts the pawns after move 8 and says what White had in return: time, then space, then a squeeze
Tries six of White's moves (11.Qf5, 14.e5, 26.Bxf8, 36.h5, 43.Rd6, 49.Rf6) before seeing them and compares each with the engine's first choice at depth 16
Names the break the cramped side needs (here ...c4 and ...d5), and what happened when it came
Says what it means that the engine rates the game's 21.Rd6 and the alternative 21.Rd2 within 0.4 of a pawn at depth 16, yet rates the position level at depth 20

steps.text: **AlphaZero (White) against Stockfish 8, December 2017.** Both players are programs. AlphaZero learned chess by playing itself; Stockfish 8 is a conventional engine. This is one of the example games in the paper that announced the match (arXiv 1712.01815), played at one minute per move [S]. No person chose these moves, so every "why" below is our reading, labelled [I]. Every engine number comes from a newer engine (Stockfish 19) at a stated depth: evidence, not proof.

steps.text: **The idea, with its conditions [I].** Space helps when the other side's pieces run out of good squares, not just because your pawns stand far forward. It lasts while the opponent has no pawn break to loosen the grip and your advanced pawn cannot be attacked. It fails when a break arrives, or when the pawn that took the space becomes a target. Two questions: which squares can their pieces still use, and which pawn move would undo the grip?

steps.text: **Why the trade mattered [I].** A bishop that guards the dark squares near the king is hard to replace with a pawn or a rook. Once it left the board, the queen and a rook could settle beside the king without being driven away. Znosko-Borovsky argued that a lead in space can be pressed slowly, but he warned to watch for a liberating sacrifice [V-sheet, 6.6]. The trade also costs White a bishop that was doing good work.

steps.text: **Waiting, with conditions [H].** Three of White's six moves were bishop moves and none made a threat. Waiting is safe only while two things hold: the opponent has no way to break the grip, and your own pawns and pieces stay protected. [H] Black's queen also shuffled, which may mean it had no better plan; a number cannot prove that. Before a waiting move, name the break your opponent wants and check that your move does not allow it.

steps.text: **Down in material, still better [I].** A side can be several points down and still be better when the other side's pieces cannot get into the game. Here Black's queen sits in the corner and its rooks guard pawns. Ask of any exchange sacrifice: which enemy pieces can reach the fight afterwards, and which cannot?

steps.text: **What the game shows [I].** The pawn bought time (moves 9 to 11), then space (the pawn on e5), then a squeeze (the trade at move 26, the h-pawn on h6, the queen cornered on h8). The cramped side's two breaks, ...c4 and ...d5, did not free Black. This is one game from one match of two programs [S]: it shows a pattern, not a rule, and your own games rarely give one side this much control.

steps.prompt: Teach-back: in three or four sentences, explain to a beginner how White got something for the pawn it gave up. Say when this kind of space works and when it does not (for example when the cramped side has a pawn break), give one example you could set up on a board, and one mistake to avoid. Self-check afterwards: did you say when it works and when it fails, give an example a beginner could set up, and name a mistake? The app grades nothing; compare with the recap.

steps.text:
**Recap.**
- A pawn can buy time: pieces developed and pointed at a target.
- A defended pawn that attacks a piece can gain space, while the opponent has no pawn break to undermine it.
- Trade the piece that guards the key squares.
- Waiting is safe only if you know the break you are stopping.
- Being down in material is fine if their pieces cannot join the fight.
- Engine numbers move with depth: evidence, not proof.
